title: GROUP BY, HAVING & Aggregation
interviewAnswer: GROUP BY changes the grain of the result by aggregating rows into groups. WHERE filters before aggregation; HAVING filters after aggregation.
why: Aggregation tests row-grain reasoning and is ubiquitous in analytics and feature engineering.
intuition: GROUP BY collapses rows sharing group keys. WHERE filters input rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregate values exist.
deepDive: Every selected non-aggregated column must be functionally compatible with the group grain. COUNT(*) counts rows while COUNT(column) ignores NULL. Conditional aggregation with CASE computes multiple metrics in one pass. Be careful that joins before aggregation may duplicate facts and inflate sums.
workedExample: To find customers with at least five completed orders, filter completed rows in WHERE, group by customer, then HAVING COUNT(*)>=5.
code:
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS n_orders, SUM(amount) AS revenue
FROM orders
WHERE status='completed'
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5;
commonMistakes: Using WHERE with an aggregate expression instead of HAVING.
Aggregating after a duplicate-amplifying join without checking grain.
followUps: How do you do conditional aggregation?
When would a window function be better?
production: Feature pipelines should document output grain and validate counts/sums against source totals so join/aggregation mistakes are caught early.
